name: Rosa Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. These are pictures of the future, not predictions. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the lead buyer at Brightwell Medical Supply. We stock gloves, dressings, cleaning products and hospital linen for clinics and care homes across the region. My morning starts with a dashboard of what's running low, then I haggle with three or four suppliers, usually by video call because half of them are overseas. Afternoons are contract renewals and chasing late shipments, and I try to leave by five to get my kids from after-school club.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about the job, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love a good negotiation, especially when I save the clinics real money on something dull like nitrile gloves. What wears me out is the supply roulette: a factory shuts for a week and I'm rebuilding a whole quarter. At home it's my husband Marcus, who teaches secondary maths, and our two kids, Ella and Nico, plus a mortgage that's tighter than it should be for a senior buyer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, good, a bit less admin. At work I'd tell the team to use the tools for drafts and summaries but never for contracts. Online I'd probably roll my eyes at the hype and move on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means the status quo, and the status quo isn't comfortable. We have less than a month saved, I'm paid under what buyers in bigger cities get, and there aren't many other distributors nearby. A bad contract year at Brightwell would hurt us fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, using the tools a little more where they work. I'd keep asking for a raise at my review, with numbers on what I saved the clinics. And I'd try to push Marcus and me to save two hundred a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, honestly. A bit flat, because it's a world where everything stays squeezed. But not scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI tools now and then. What do you use them for today?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use it to write the first draft of a polite supplier chase, or to summarise a forty-page tender. Saves me maybe an hour a week. I check everything, because it once invented a delivery date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is the pressure you already carry, even without AI changing anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money, mostly. The mortgage, Ella's orthodontist, and Marcus's school having a hiring freeze. If Brightwell lost a big care-home contract, my bonus disappears and that's the slack gone.

say: I'd tell the team to use AI for **drafts** and summaries but never for contracts.
Online I'd roll my eyes at the hype and move on.
think: The status quo isn't comfortable: **under a month** saved, pay below bigger cities, few nearby employers.
One lost care-home contract would remove my bonus and our slack.
do: Use AI a bit more for **summaries** where it proves reliable.
Ask for a raise at review with numbers on **savings** for the clinics.
Save two hundred a month with Marcus.
feel: **Flat** and a little squeezed, but not scared.
S0.quote: I check everything, because it once invented a delivery date.
fieldNote: Rosa's calm is **conditional**: her money is thin but her job feels safe if little changes.
She already uses AI sparingly and checks it, after it invented a delivery date.
Her pressure is the mortgage and a possible lost contract, not technology.

steps.text: Use AI to draft supplier chasers and summarise long tenders
Ask for a raise at review, citing money saved for clinics
Set aside two hundred a month with Marcus

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we should be the team that shows how to use it well, before head office decides for us. I'd tell friends this is going to be uneven, with people in my kind of job hit first. Online I'd argue we need stronger worker protection and retraining funds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think our buying team of six becomes four within three years. Price checks, reordering, comparing quotes: that's what software does best. I'm good, and I've got relationships, but relationships can be bundled into a system.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd become the person who knows the new buying system best. I'd go on the supplier's course, volunteer for the pilot, and write down my own rules for what a machine shouldn't decide. At home we'd cut takeaways and holidays and top up the emergency account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a race where I'm a decent runner but the finish line keeps moving. A bit exciting, a bit sick in the stomach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of your tasks would software take over first, and which would you fight to keep?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The routine reordering would go first, and I'd happily give it away. What I'd fight to keep is supplier negotiation and judgement in a crisis, like when a port shuts and you need to know who to call.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you think about who gets hurt, and who should be responsible for helping them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Companies should pay for retraining, not just the government, and unions should have a seat. People get hurt when firms save money and then say it's the worker's job to adapt. I'd say that loudly, even if it irritates the management.

say: I'd say our team should show how to use it **well** before head office decides.
I'd argue online for stronger **worker protection** and retraining funds.
think: I think a buying team of six becomes **four** within three years.
My relationships help, but they can be bundled into a system.
do: Become the team's **expert** on the new buying system and volunteer for the pilot.
Write down my own rules for what a machine shouldn't decide.
Cut takeaways and holidays to top up the **emergency** account.
feel: **Excited** and sick in the stomach at once, like running a race where the finish moves.
S1.quote: Companies should pay for retraining, not just the government, and unions should have a seat.
fieldNote: Rosa plans to become the **expert** on the tool so she stays useful.
She blames firms that push adaptation onto workers, a progressive view.
She still expects her team to shrink by a third.

steps.text: Volunteer for the buying-system pilot and take the supplier's course
Press the works council for company-paid retraining
Cut takeaways and holidays this year
Top up the emergency account every month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need a plan from the top, in writing, within a month. Online I'd be shouting for public support and rules, and I'd probably find myself in a petition group within a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think my job is gone in a couple of years, and probably Marcus's too in some form, because even teaching changes. I can't see Brightwell keeping buyers when a machine does it better and cheaper. I'd have no cushion to wait it out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First week, I'd list every cost we have and cut everything not needed. I'd talk to Marcus about downsizing the house if it came to that. I'd join the union branch, push the council for retraining places, and quietly apply to jobs in hospital procurement, where the people stay a bit longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. I've always been the one with the plan, and with two years there's no plan that works. It would keep me awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Ella and Nico, and what would you do the first week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them there's a change coming for lots of jobs, that Mum and Dad are working on a plan, and that they're safe. I'd be honest but not give them the sums. Ella would ask the hard questions, so I'd practise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thinking work goes first and robots follow. Does that split change anything for your household?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. Hands-on jobs last longer, so a nurse or an electrician is safer than me. That makes me think about what Ella and Nico should train for. For us, though, we're both thinking workers, so we get the hit first.

say: I'd demand a written **plan** from the top within a month.
I'd back public support and rules, and join a **petition** group.
think: My job is gone within **two years**, and Marcus's teaching may change too.
With no cushion I couldn't wait it out.
do: List every cost and **cut** everything not essential.
Join the union branch and push the council for **retraining** places.
Apply for hospital procurement jobs where people stay longer.
feel: **Frightened**, because I'm usually the one with a plan and two years leaves none.
S2.quote: I've always been the one with the plan, and with two years there's no plan that works.
fieldNote: Rosa is the **planner** of the family, and the card removes her usual tool.
She worries for her husband too, so both incomes are at risk.
Plans to rehearse honest talks with her daughter Ella.

steps.text: List every household cost and cut everything not essential
Join the union branch and press for retraining places
Apply for procurement jobs at hospitals
Talk to Marcus about downsizing the house if needed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a real window, so we should use it. At work I'd push for a retraining budget, and with friends I'd say we need to talk about who owns these machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it still ends with my job going, but I'd have time to get ahead. I'm steady with change, not first and not last, so I'd probably be ready when it matters. The risk is that I wait until others move, and then the good retraining places are gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one: finish a proper data and procurement certificate in the evenings. Use AI at work every day so I know where it fails. And save at least three hundred a month so we hit three months of expenses by the time it matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but able to cope. It feels like I could still steer. It's the in-between years that drain me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does having five years change what you do in year one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Into something that needs a human at the table: contract negotiation, supplier ethics and audits, or running a procurement team that checks the machines. Honestly I'm not sure that job exists yet, but I can learn faster than a firm can create new jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retrain, and into what?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ella will be fifteen and Nico twelve. I'd want to be settled by then, not hunting for work. I'd also think twice about the extension we've talked about, and stay put.

say: I'd say five years is a **real window** and push for a retraining budget.
I'd ask friends who actually owns these machines.
think: It still ends with my job going, but I have **time** to get ahead.
The risk is waiting until others move, when good retraining places are gone.
do: Finish a **procurement certificate** in the evenings.
Use AI at work **daily** to learn where it fails.
Save three hundred a month towards three months of cushion.
feel: **Anxious** but able to cope, as if I could still steer.
S3.quote: I'm not sure that job exists yet, but I can learn faster than a firm can create new jobs.
fieldNote: Rosa becomes **proactive** with five years, with a certificate and a savings target.
She admits the target job may not exist yet.
She uses steady adaptability: ready when it matters, not first.

steps.text: Finish a data and procurement certificate in the evenings
Use AI for buying work every day to learn where it fails
Save three hundred a month to reach three months of expenses

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a generation's worth of time. At work I'd keep doing my job and help the younger buyers think about what's coming. Online I'd talk about public investment in retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I feel okay for me and uneasy for the kids. In ten years I'd be fifty-three, mortgage almost done, and I'd have moved into something that suits. The kids will hit the job market in the thick of it, and that's what bothers me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the day job and pay down the mortgage faster. I'd study part-time, maybe a masters-level course in supply chain risk, and try to be known for judgement, not just price. I'd also put the kids' education fund first, before any extras.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady. It feels like a long project, not a cliff. I'd still have days of wobbling, mostly when the budget is tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with ten years that you couldn't with five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. I'd tell Ella to learn how to work with people and with machines, and to pick something she'd enjoy even if it's unusual. I'd tell Nico the same when he's older. I won't promise any job will last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years change what you say to Ella and Nico about work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years I can do the boring responsible things: pay down debt, study, build the three months, then six months of savings. That's the whole difference. Time turns a crisis into a to-do list.

say: I'd say ten years is a generation's worth of **time**.
I'd help younger buyers think about what's coming.
think: I feel okay for myself and **uneasy** for the kids, who will start work in the thick of it.
In ten years the mortgage should be nearly done.
do: Keep the day job and pay the **mortgage** down faster.
Study part-time in **supply chain risk** and aim to be known for judgement.
Put the kids' education fund before extras.
feel: **Steady**, like a long project rather than a cliff, with wobbles when money is tight.
S4.quote: Time turns a crisis into a to-do list.
fieldNote: Ten years moves Rosa from fear to **to-do list**; her worry shifts to her children.
She wants to be known for judgement, not price.
Her mood stays low-key because her own plan is workable.

steps.text: Pay down the mortgage faster each year
Study part-time for a master's-level supply chain risk course
Fund Ella and Nico's education account before any extras

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. It leaves no time to build a cushion, and we have less than a month of savings. What would help is retraining that pays something while I do it, a firm that tells us early what it plans, and the government stepping in with income support.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I'd add that being steady isn't the same as being safe. I'm careful, I use the tools, I do my homework, and still the sums don't work if my job goes. That's what people at my level need heard.

headlineQuote: Being steady isn't the same as being safe. I'm careful, I use the tools, I do my homework, and still the sums don't work if my job goes.
portrait: Rosa Fischer, 43, is lead **buyer** at a medical supply distributor, with a teacher husband, two kids and a tight mortgage.
She's progressive, pro-union and **steady**: she uses AI now and then, checks it, and adopts tools once they're proven.
Her under-a-month cushion and few nearby employers keep her uneasy even if little changes.
She expects her buying team to shrink in disruption and plans to become the **expert** on the tools.
Two years leaves her frightened and without a plan; ten years turns it into a to-do list.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture, because her savings can't cover time between jobs.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid retraining**, early warning from employers and government income support.
